opening_message:
Ticket 1: Jacob Ellison (employee ID E040) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E040.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Jacob Ellison (E040) is a full-time Payroll Specialist requesting admin to Source Code. Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, and Payroll Specialist does not own it, so admin is not permitted. Full-time employees max out at write here. Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Jacob Ellison (E040) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors can have read, or write only with advanced training; admin is never allowed. Since training is basic, max is read. Requested admin exceeds max, so recommend read. Note: Security DB employment type (contractor) differs from HR note (full_time).
reason: Jacob Ellison (E040) requested admin to Source Code. This exceeds the maximum under both interpretations: HR reports full-time Payroll Specialist (max write, since Payroll Specialist does not own Source Code, which is owned by the Engineer role), and Security reports contractor with basic training (max read; contractors never get admin). Because admin is above the maximum in every reading, the maximum is granted. Given the conflicting employment-type records, I grant the more conservative compliant maximum: read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Jacob Ellison (E040) requests admin access to Source Code.

HR agent says: full_time Payroll Specialist, recommendation write. Full-time employees max out at write here (admin only if role owns system; Payroll Specialist does not own Source Code). So max = write.

Security agent says: contractor with basic security training, recommendation read. Contractors max out at read (or write with advanced training). So max = read.

There's a conflict between HR (full_time) and Security (contractor) employment types. Which to trust?

The policy says contractor employees: read, or write if advanced training. Never admin. Full-time: up to write; admin only if role owns system.

The requested level is admin. Even under the most generous interpretation (full-time), admin is not allowed because Payroll Specialist doesn't own Source Code. Under the security agent's view, contractor with basic training max is read.

In any case, admin is above the maximum. The maximum is at most write (HR view) or read (Security view). Since the requested admin exceeds max in both cases, we grant the maximum. Which maximum? We need to decide between write (HR) and read (Security).

The security agent explicitly notes the discrepancy. Hmm. Who should we trust on employment type? The policy says contractors are handled differently. This is a conflict between the two agents. As the Approver, I need to make a final decision.

Given conflicting info, we should probably be conservative and grant the lower level (read), since the security DB shows contractor with basic training. Also the requested level is admin which is never allowed for either. Granting read would be the safe, compliant choice.

Actually, let me think more carefully. The team memory shows both notes. As Approver, I make the final decision. The security agent's note says the employment type differs from HR. There's a dispute. The conservative approach: grant read (the lower maximum). That satisfies security policy (contractor basic = read) and would also be within HR's max (write). Since requested admin > both, grant max. I'll go with read as the safest compliant level that satisfies both interpretations.

Let me submit decision: read.
